answer_summary: A National Weather Service-declared derecho passed through the Columbus, Ohio area on June 13-14, 2022.
Forced transmission outages reduced the local network while hot, humid post-storm conditions raised demand, heavily loading the remaining facilities.
AEP and PJM first used transmission reconfiguration and generation redispatch, then implemented demand response and directed firm-load reductions when system issues persisted.
PJM used 100 MW of demand response and shed 500 MW and 450 MW of firm load on June 14 and 15; this relieved constraints and kept the BES reliable.

Crews used relay distance-to-fault information to locate affected sections, trimmed vegetation, and restored lines; the report also suggests using post-storm LIDAR to identify changed vegetation encroachments and temporary limits.
Reportable losses of SCADA, ICCP, RTU, AGC, state estimator, or real-time contingency analysis lasting at least 30 minutes formed the assessed mechanism.
Management/Organization was the leading root-cause category, covering weaknesses in management methods, resources, planning, supervision, and change management.
Loss or degradation of SCADA removes operators' visibility of device status and critical substation data and their ability to remotely operate breakers and switches.
The 2018–2020 EMS losses did not cause loss of generation, transmission lines, or customer load.
Recommended practices included current grid models, physically independent redundant circuits and support, standardized network settings with network separation, and robust alarm assessment.
The assessment covered losses of SCADA, ICCP, RTU, AGC, SE, or RTCA lasting at least 30 minutes; SE/RTCA loss was the most prevalent in 2018-2019.
Management/Organization was the leading root-cause category; explicit contributing problems included external modeling, improper network configuration, and loss of power supply.
SCADA loss deprives operators of device and critical substation indications and remote breaker or switch control, making it the likely most operationally impactful EMS failure.
The 2018–2019 EMS losses did not directly cause generation, transmission-line, or customer-load loss.
Mitigations included maintaining models, ensuring physically separate redundant services and support, assessing alarm failure modes and secure power, and completing software testing.
Winter Storm Elliott, described as a bomb cyclone or extratropical cyclone, moved east from the upper Plains and blanketed most of the eastern United States on December 23-24, 2022.

Extreme cold caused natural-gas wellhead freeze-offs and other frozen equipment, while the cold weather also prevented needed maintenance, producing major gas-production declines that constrained generation fuel supply.

Operators curtailed non-firm exports, declared emergency alerts, deployed load-modifying resources and reserves, curtailed emergency exports, and ultimately shed firm load where reserves were depleted.
At the worst point 90,500 MW of generation was simultaneously unavailable or derated, and the capacity shortage caused 5,400 MW of firm load shed.

Mitigation included advance cold-weather preparation notices, curtailing non-firm exports, using load-modifying resources, and rebalancing through more generation, export curtailment, or firm-load reduction when supply could not increase.

Winter Storm Elliott caused significant generation loss and unprecedented Eastern Interconnection firm-load shedding, including outages of more than 150 blackstart-designated units totaling about 19,000 MW.

Blackstart resources could be unavailable because they lack firm gas supply or transportation, cold degrades substation batteries, or generator cold-weather-critical components freeze and prevent starting or operation.
Recommendation 3 directed a joint NERC-Regional Entity study with FERC staff to assess blackstart-unit availability and readiness under extreme cold across the Eastern and Western Interconnections.
More than 150 blackstart units representing about 19,000 MW were outaged, raising serious concern that they could not perform their restoration role after a blackout.

Mitigation includes systematically assessing each blackstart resource's cold-critical components, pre-positioning backup generators at key gas facilities, staffing compressor and control sites during extreme cold, and arranging stored gas for reliable restoration fuel.
The follow-up arose from December 2022 Winter Storm Elliott, which caused widespread power outages and other problems in the eastern United States.

The EFAM example identifies extreme weather and tight forecast resource-adequacy margins as conditions requiring closer forecast review, with demand response needing to be reflected correctly in actual-load data.
NERC's RSTC convened a panel and invited eight stakeholders to present load-forecasting changes and improvements made in response to the Elliott recommendations.
The follow-up identified load forecasting as the subject of two of the Elliott report's eleven recommendations.

Stakeholders described closer human monitoring and adjustment of weather and demand forecasts, joint capacity planning, committing additional generation during extreme events, and site-specific cold-weather plans with accountable owners.
Winter Storm Elliott's extreme cold caused generation outages and unavailability that threatened BES reliability.
The underlying reliability problem was resource adequacy, not low system inertia.
The largest observed generation trip was about 880 MW and reduced Eastern Interconnection frequency from 59.986 to 59.95 Hz, a typical decline for a trip of that size.
UFLS would not have triggered even for a modeled 10,000 MW loss, and the system maintained dynamic stability.
Fast governor response and load sensitivity limited frequency decline, while the joint FERC-NERC inquiry identified outage causes and issued preventive industry recommendations.
Hurricane Helene triggered the largest 2024 transmission outage event.
Hurricane Helene's weather damage drove the event; at least the longest 100-199 kV circuit outage was explicitly attributed to a fallen tree that likely caused extensive structural damage.
The event affected 20 transmission owners in 10 states and produced 431 automatic outages: 422 ac-circuit and 9 transformer outages across 413 distinct TADS elements.
Helene caused 431 outages affecting 9,138 miles and 127,687 MVA; cumulative loss was 1,140 element-days and 288,329 MVA-days.
Restoration peaked at 6.8 restores per hour after 11.6 hours, slowed to 3.1 per hour by halfway and 0.37 per hour near 95%, with 95% of outages restored after 182 hours.
A transmission-line fault triggered the simultaneous data-center load disconnection.
Approximately 1,500 MW of data-center load disconnected simultaneously and unexpectedly, creating an abrupt load step comparable to a large nuclear plant coming online.
System voltage and frequency rose rapidly after the load disconnection, although the overall BES effect remained limited.
The 1,500 MW load loss created excess-generation imbalance comparable to suddenly adding a large nuclear unit; voltage and frequency rose, but total BES impact was limited.
Reliability planning needs accurate models of data-center behavior during faults and resources positioned to rebalance the system quickly after rapid load changes.
A single-line-to-ground fault on a 345 kV transmission circuit in southern Nevada/southwest Utah initiated the April 10, 2023 disturbance.
Solar output fell because inverters tripped on loss of synchronization, ac overvoltage, or ac overcurrent.
The line outage did not trip conventional generation, but inverter trips across the area caused a significant aggregate solar-PV output drop.
Approximately 929 MW of solar generation was lost, with individual-site reductions ranging from 3 MW to 234 MW.
Owners were advised to work with inverter manufacturers on known ride-through-setting improvements; implemented changes kept inverters from tripping and improved recovery to two or three minutes.
Extreme cold temperatures and freezing precipitation from February 8-20, 2021 initiated the generating-unit outages across Texas and the South Central United States.
Lack of cold-weather preparedness and interruptions to natural-gas supply reduced resource availability, and increasing fleet dependence on gas magnified the effects.
To prevent cascading outages and system-wide blackouts, ERCOT ordered up to 20,000 MW of firm-load shedding, while SPP and MISO shed another combined 3,418 MW.
The event produced a U.S.-record 23,418 MW of controlled firm-load shed, at least 210 deaths, and an estimated $80-$130 billion loss to the Texas economy.

Mitigation focused on mandatory generator winterization, fuel assurance and energy-resource adequacy, natural-gas infrastructure cold reliability, joint winter-peak preparedness, and emergency and seasonal cold-weather operations.
Transmission-system disturbances triggered widespread loss of BPS-connected inverter-based resources.
Most inverters disconnected because sub-cycle transient overvoltages activated instantaneous inverter protection.
Fault-event transients caused many inverters to trip offline and a significant additional share to enter momentary cessation during and after the faults.
The report classified the widespread loss of BPS-connected inverter-based resources during transmission disturbances as an emerging reliability risk.
NERC used a task force, event analysis and industry webinars, a Level II alert, and a proposed reliability guideline covering planning, design, coordination, and inverter performance.
Smoke from the Blue Cut wildfire caused two 500 kV transmission lines to trip on August 16, 2016.
Dispersed solar facilities stopped injecting power because their inverters erroneously calculated system frequency near 57 Hz during the fault.

Two smoke-induced 500 kV faults cleared as designed, but utility-scale renewable resources, primarily solar, then disconnected practically instantaneously while conventional generators remained online.
The line outages caused a noticeable frequency excursion and the nearly instantaneous loss of more than 1,000 MW across multiple renewable resources, with no conventional generator trip.
The ERO requested an event report and worked with CAISO and Southern California Edison engineers and planners to investigate the first major transmission-disturbance-related renewable loss.
ERCOT experienced one frequency event in which measured frequency response fell slightly below its interconnection frequency-response obligation.
The documented deficiency was measured ERCOT frequency response slightly below its IFRO.
Contracted load-resource reserves tripped on low frequency and more than compensated for the response shortfall.
ERCOT's measured response was slightly below IFRO, but supplemental load-resource reserves were more than adequate.
Precontracted load-resource reserves designed to trip at low frequency supplemented and exceeded the needed response.
A lightning-strike-induced fault at one terminal of a 345 kV transmission line initiated the protection-system event.
The lightning-fault transient caused both System 1 and System 2 protection groups to shut down.
With neither local protection group clearing the fault, it persisted for more than 1.5 seconds until remote-terminal time-delayed protection operated.
The immediate impact was failure of both local relay systems to clear the 345 kV fault, extending fault duration beyond 1.5 seconds.
Protection at the remote line terminals tripped as designed using time-delayed elements and cleared the fault.
